mainTopic: Attached versus detached blades in שחיטה, direct versus indirect force, and the status of something detached and later attached
overview: The גמרא finishes resolving a ברייתא whose two clauses seem to clash, and proves that a blade attached from the start differs from one that was detached and later reattached. It then explains why one source calls שחיטה with a machine (מוכני) valid while another calls it invalid. The first answer contrasts a potter's wheel with a waterwheel. The second answer contrasts direct force (כח ראשון) with indirect force (כח שני), backed by רב פפא's ruling that someone who drowns another person with released water is liable only through direct force, since anything else is only גרמא. Next, רבי offers a פסוק from the עקידה as a source that שחיטה needs a detached knife. רבי חייא dismisses it, because the פסוק only shows אברהם's eagerness. רבא then says that for עבודה זרה, something detached and later attached clearly counts as detached, while for הכשר זרעים it is a dispute between תנאים. He proves this from a משנה about a bowl turned over on a wall. רבי אלעזר says two תנאים wrote that משנה, while רב פפא reads it as one תנא who distinguishes a cave wall from a built wall. The amud ends as רבא begins a new question, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The two clauses of the teaching contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the two halves of the ברייתא seem to clash.
steps.simpleTranslation: These two clauses contradict each other!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says that the first part and the last part of the ברייתא it was just reading seem to contradict each other. This is the setup for the resolution in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One clause calls שחיטה with an attached blade valid. The other clause calls it invalid. Both are in the same ברייתא, so they cannot simply be two opinions arguing. There must be a difference between the cases.

keyTerms.meaning: They contradict each other (two statements that cannot both be true as they stand)

phrases.english: They are difficult, contradicting each other!
phrases.notes: This is about the two clauses of the ברייתא from just before: one says the שחיטה is valid, the other says it is not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the analysis of the ברייתא from the previous part of the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the ברייתא about slaughtering with an attached blade.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same source cannot call the same act both valid and invalid unless the cases are different.

steps.title: Attached from the start versus cut off and reattached
steps.stepSummary: The contradiction proves that something attached from the start is treated differently from something cut off and later reattached.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, must we not learn from this that there is a difference between something attached from the start and something cut off and later reattached? Yes, learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction. One clause is about a blade that was always attached to the ground. The other is about a blade that was detached and later reattached. The גמרא then confirms this as a proven conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only way both clauses of the ברייתא can be right is if they describe different cases. So the ברייתא itself becomes a proof that מחובר מעיקרו and תלוש ולבסוף חברו follow different rules. The closing שמע מינה confirms that this reading stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not that... (introduces the only reasonable way to explain the source)
Attached from the start (something that grew in or was always part of the ground)
Detached and later reattached by a person
Learn from it (a proof is confirmed)

steps.whatToRemember: A blade that was attached from the start (מחובר מעיקרו) is different from one that was detached and later reattached (תלוש ולבסוף חברו). The contradiction inside the ברייתא proves this.

phrases.english: Rather, must one not learn from it
that there is a difference between something attached from the outset
and something detached that he ultimately reattached?
Indeed, learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 1 and turns it into a proof.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: מחובר מעיקרו and תלוש ולבסוף חברו have different halachic status in this context.

steps.title: Quoting the ruling that slaughtering with a machine is valid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes another line of the ברייתא: שחיטה done with a mechanical wheel is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: One who slaughters with a machine, his שחיטה is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to quote a new line from the ברייתא so it can discuss it. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מוכני is a wheel with a knife attached to it. The ruling says that slaughtering with it is kosher, even though the wheel's motion does the cutting. This opens a new topic.

keyTerms.meaning: A mechanism; a wheel with a knife attached
His slaughter is valid

phrases.english: The Master said:
One who slaughters with a mechanism
phrases.notes: Picture a wheel with a knife fixed to it, so the turning wheel does the cutting.

phrases.english: his slaughter is valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: הַשּׁוֹחֵט בְּמוּכְנִי שְׁחִיטָתוֹ כְּשֵׁרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting another line of the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שחיטה performed with a mechanical wheel is valid.

steps.title: Another teaching says machine slaughter is invalid
steps.stepSummary: A different ברייתא rules that slaughtering with a machine is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it taught that his שחיטה is invalid?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling by quoting another ברייתא that says the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two sources discuss the same case, a מוכני, and reach opposite results. The גמרא now has to show how the two sources can both be correct.

keyTerms.meaning: His slaughter is invalid

phrases.english: But isn't it taught:
his slaughter is invalid!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges the ruling quoted in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that שחיטה with a מוכני is valid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A contradicting ברייתא declares the same act invalid.

steps.title: Potter's wheel versus waterwheel
steps.stepSummary: The valid case uses a potter's wheel, which a person moves. The invalid case uses a waterwheel, which water moves.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this one is about a potter's wheel, and that one is about a waterwheel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two sources describe different kinds of wheels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person turns a potter's wheel with a foot pedal, so the cutting comes from the person's own force, and the שחיטה is valid. A waterwheel is turned by the water, not by a person, so the שחיטה is invalid. The key question is whether a human's force did the cutting.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (introduces an answer that splits the cases)
A potter's wheel, turned by a person
A waterwheel, turned by flowing water

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is with a potter's wheel,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that says valid: the potter's own foot turns the wheel.

phrases.english: that is with a waterwheel.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּסַרְנָא דְּפַחְרָא, הָא בְּסַרְנָא דְּמַיָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the sources refer to different devices.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seem to discuss the same machine and disagree.
steps.terutzMaskana: Human-powered wheel = valid; water-powered wheel = invalid.

steps.title: Both cases are waterwheels: first turn versus second turn
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: both cases use a waterwheel. The cut on the first turn is valid, and the cut on a later turn is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you wish, say: both are about a waterwheel, and it is not difficult. This one is with first force, and that one is with second force.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer. Both sources discuss a waterwheel, but they differ in when the knife cuts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the knife cuts on the first turn, caused right away by the person releasing the water (כח ראשון), that counts as the person's action, so the שחיטה is valid. If it cuts only on a later turn (כח שני), the person's action is too far removed, so the שחיטה is invalid. This answer says even a waterwheel can be valid if the force is direct.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces an alternative answer)
This and that; both cases
First or direct force, coming straight from the person's action
Second or indirect force, one step removed from the person

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think this answer agrees with the first one that a waterwheel is always invalid. Here a waterwheel can be valid, as long as the cut happens through כח ראשון.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
this and that are both with a waterwheel,
and it is not difficult:
this is with primary force,
phrases.notes: The person lets the water go, and the knife cuts on the wheel's very first turn.

phrases.english: that is with secondary force.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא בְּסַרְנָא דְּמַיָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the same contradiction from step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative splitting of cases: same device, different stage of force.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A waterwheel might always be invalid because water, not the person, turns it.
steps.terutzMaskana: A cut through כח ראשון counts as the person's act (valid); a cut through כח שני does not (invalid).
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the important line between direct force (כח ראשון) and indirect force (כח שני), which matters in many areas of halacha.

steps.title: רב פפא: drowning someone with a stream of water
steps.stepSummary: A parallel ruling: if someone ties up another person and sends a stream of water at him and he dies, the one who sent the water is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is like what רב פפא said: Someone who tied up another person and sent a stream of water onto him, and he died, is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a parallel ruling from רב פפא about murder to support the idea of כח ראשון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Releasing water that directly kills someone is treated as the person's own act, so he is liable. This matches the second answer, where releasing water that turns the wheel and cuts right away counts as the person's own שחיטה.

keyTerms.meaning: And like this (introduces a parallel case)
He tied him up
A stream or channel of water
Liable (here, for murder)

phrases.english: And like that which Rav Pappa said:
A person who tied up his fellow
and diverted a stream of water onto him
and he died, is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the second answer (step 6) with a parallel from the laws of murder.
steps.raayaObject: The distinction between כח ראשון and כח שני.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב פפא's ruling on killing someone with a stream of water.

steps.title: Why is he liable?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב פפא's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the person is liable, since the water, not his hand, killed the victim. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It seems surprising to call someone a killer when the water did the work. The answer will show what makes an act count as the person's own.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why releasing water counts as the person's own act of killing.

steps.title: The water is like his own arrows
steps.stepSummary: He is liable because the water acted like his own arrows that struck the victim.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is his arrows that took effect on him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the water is like arrows the person shot. It is his weapon, so the killing is his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Shooting an arrow counts as killing even though the arrow travels on its own after it leaves your hand. In the same way, water a person releases straight at the victim is treated as his own direct force.

keyTerms.meaning: His own arrows; force that comes directly from the person
Took effect, was effective

phrases.english: It is his arrows
phrases.notes: Like someone who shoots an arrow: once it leaves his hand it flies by itself, but he is still the killer.

phrases.english: that took effect on him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The water is considered the person's own arrows (גירי דידיה), so the act is his.

steps.title: Liable only for direct force; indirect force is only גרמא
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא's ruling applies only to כח ראשון. With כח שני, the death is only indirectly caused (גרמא), and he is not liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this applies with first force, but with second force it is merely indirect causation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits רב פפא's ruling. The person is liable only when the water hits the victim through direct force. If it reaches him through indirect force, it is just גרמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is exactly the line the second answer used for the waterwheel. כח ראשון counts as the person's action, so he is liable for murder and the שחיטה is valid. כח שני is only גרמא, so he is exempt and the שחיטה is invalid.

keyTerms.meaning: And these words apply only... (introduces a limit on a rule)
Merely indirect causation, which does not count as the person's own act

steps.whatToRemember: כח ראשון counts as the person's own act: he is liable for murder, and the שחיטה is valid. כח שני is only גרמא: he is exempt, and the שחיטה is invalid.
steps.whyThisMatters: The difference between כח ראשון and גרמא is a key idea that comes up across many areas of halacha, such as נזיקין, murder, and שחיטה.

phrases.english: And this applies with primary force,
phrases.notes: Here the victim is close by, and the released water hits him right away.

phrases.english: but with secondary force,
it is merely indirect causation.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי בְּכֹחַ רִאשׁוֹן, אֲבָל בְּכֹחַ שֵׁנִי גְּרָמָא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב פפא's ruling and links it back to the waterwheel answer in step 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Only direct force (כח ראשון) is attributed to the person; indirect force (כח שני) is גרמא and is not his act.

steps.title: רבי derives that slaughter needs a detached blade
steps.stepSummary: The scene is set: רב sits behind רבי חייא, who sits before רבי. רבי teaches that שחיטה must be done with a detached blade, based on the פסוק "and he took the knife to slaughter."
steps.simpleTranslation: רב sat behind רבי חייא, and רבי חייא sat before רבי. רבי sat and said: From where do we know that slaughter must be done with something detached? Because it says, "And he took the knife to slaughter."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story. רבי gives a source from a פסוק that שחיטה must be done with a detached knife, not with a blade that is attached to the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps dealt with blades attached to a wheel or to the ground. Here רבי offers a פסוק as the source for the rule. Because אברהם 'took' the knife, רבי learns that the knife must be something you can pick up.

keyTerms.meaning: Detached; not connected to the ground
Knife (the word used in the story of עקידת יצחק)
Kosher ritual slaughter

phrases.english: Rav sat behind Rabbi Chiya,
and Rabbi Chiya sat before Rebbi,
phrases.notes: "רבי" means רבי יהודה הנשיא, who put together the משנה.

phrases.english: and Rebbi sat and said:
From where do we know that slaughter is done with something detached?
As it says: "And he took the knife to slaughter."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion: a scriptural source for the rule of a detached blade.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שחיטה must be done with a detached blade, learned from "ויקח את המאכלת לשחוט."

steps.title: רב asks what רבי meant
steps.stepSummary: רב quietly asks רבי חייא what רבי is saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to רבי חייא: What is he saying?
steps.whatsHappening: רב does not understand how the פסוק proves the rule, so he asks רבי חייא. This sets up רבי חייא's reply in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question points to a gap in the proof. The story of the עקידה does not obviously teach anything about how kosher slaughter must be done.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he saying? (a request to explain a statement)

phrases.english: Rav said to Rabbi Chiya:
What is he saying?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the proof that was just given.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How does the פסוק prove that שחיטה needs a detached blade?

steps.title: רבי חייא calls the proof meaningless
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא answers that רבי's proof is like a ו scratched on a rough tree trunk: it means nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He is saying something like a ו written on a tree trunk.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא answers רב, and his answer rejects רבי's proof. The rule may still be true, but this פסוק is not a real source for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mark scratched on rough bark looks like a letter but tells you nothing. In the same way, רבי's proof looks like a source but does not actually prove the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A rough tree trunk
The letter ו

phrases.english: He said to him:
He is saying something like a vav written on a tree trunk.
phrases.notes: A scratch on rough bark might look like a ו but means nothing. That is what he thinks of this proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב's question by dismissing רבי's derivation.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the scriptural proof is rejected, not the rule of a detached blade itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The פסוק does not actually support the rule.

steps.title: But רבי quoted a verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי חייא: how can you call it meaningless when רבי quoted a פסוק?
steps.simpleTranslation: But he quoted a verse!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against רבי חייא. A proof from a פסוק seems strong, so why throw it out?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is that רבי did not just give a reason of his own. He brought words of the תורה, and those seem to support his point.

keyTerms.meaning: A verse from תנ״ך
But surely (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: But he quoted a verse!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי חייא's rejection.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's dismissal of the proof
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A proof based on a פסוק cannot simply be called meaningless.

steps.title: The verse shows אברהם's eagerness
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is not teaching a law of שחיטה. It shows how eager אברהם was to do what he was told.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse is teaching us אברהם's eagerness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the פסוק is not a proof. Its message is about אברהם's eagerness, not about how kosher slaughter must be done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'he took the knife' have their own purpose in the story. Once the פסוק has that purpose, we cannot also draw a law about detached blades from it, so the proof falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Eagerness; doing a מצוה quickly and with energy
It is teaching us

steps.whatToRemember: רבי's פסוק is set aside because it only shows אברהם's eagerness. The question of a source for the detached blade stays open.

phrases.english: The verse, the eagerness of Avraham
is what it is teaching us.

steps.triggerLanguage: קְרָא זְרִיזוּתֵיהּ דְּאַבְרָהָם קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge and defends רבי חייא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The פסוק is given a different purpose.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק teaches that שחיטה needs a detached blade.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק teaches אברהם's eagerness and gives no law about שחיטה.

steps.title: רבא: for idolatry, detached-then-attached counts as detached
steps.stepSummary: רבא says it is obvious that an item which was detached and later attached to the ground counts as detached when it comes to עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is obvious to me that something detached and then attached counts as detached regarding idol worship.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא takes up a related question: what is the status of something that was once loose and was later fixed to the ground? He starts with עבודה זרה, where he says the answer is clear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to blades fixed to the ground. If such a blade counts as detached, it might be fine for שחיטה. רבא first shows a clear case before moving to a case that is disputed.

keyTerms.meaning: Detached and later attached to the ground
Idol worship
It is obvious to me

phrases.english: Rava said: It is obvious to me
that something detached that was later attached,
regarding idol worship, counts as detached,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a related topic: the status of something detached and later attached.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For עבודה זרה, something that was detached and later attached counts as detached.

steps.title: Proof: bowing to a house forbids it
steps.stepSummary: Bowing to one's house makes it forbidden. If a house counted as attached, it could not become forbidden, because the תורה says the mountains are not their gods.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Master said: One who bows to his house has made it forbidden. And if you think it counts as attached, the verse says "their gods upon the mountains," meaning the mountains are not their gods.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא proves his point. A house is built from loose stones that were later attached, and we know it can become forbidden through idol worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Things that are naturally attached to the ground, like mountains, cannot become forbidden as idols. A house can become forbidden, so stones that were later attached must still count as detached.

keyTerms.meaning: One who bows down (in worship)
He made it forbidden
Attached to the ground
And if you would think

phrases.english: As the Master said:
One who bows to his house has made it forbidden,
and if you would think it counts as attached,
"Their gods, upon the mountains"
but the mountains are not their gods.
phrases.notes: Things attached to the ground can't become forbidden as idols, so the house would never become forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר מָר הַמִּשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לְבַיִת שֶׁלּוֹ אֲסָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the proof for רבא's statement.
steps.raayaObject: Something detached and later attached counts as detached for עבודה זרה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rule that bowing to a house forbids it, together with the פסוק "אלהיהם על ההרים."

steps.title: For making produce susceptible, it is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that for הכשר זרעים, the status of something detached and later attached is a dispute between תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Regarding making seeds susceptible to impurity, it is a dispute between תנאים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא moves to a second area of law. Here, unlike עבודה זרה, the answer is not obvious, because תנאים disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Produce can become ready to receive טומאה only through water that came onto it in a way the owner wanted. The question is whether water that touched something detached and later attached counts like water on a loose item.

keyTerms.meaning: Making produce able to become impure (through contact with liquid)
It is a dispute between תנאים

phrases.english: Regarding making seeds susceptible, it is a dispute between Tannaim,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same question to a second area of law, where the answer is disputed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For הכשר זרעים, the status of something detached and later attached depends on a dispute between תנאים.

steps.title: The משנה of the bowl on the wall
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says: if someone turns a bowl over on a wall so the bowl gets rinsed, the water counts under "כי יותן." If he did it so the wall won't be damaged, it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: One who turns a bowl over on a wall so that it will be rinsed, this falls under "when water is placed." If he did it so the wall won't be damaged, it does not fall under "when water is placed."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings the משנה that is the source of the תנאים dispute. Whether the rainwater can make produce susceptible depends on why the person put the bowl there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he wants the water, to rinse his bowl, it counts as water he wanted. If he only wants to protect the wall, he does not want the water, so it does not make produce susceptible. A wall is something attached, which is why this משנה matters for רבא's question.

keyTerms.meaning: One who turns a bowl upside down
"When [water] is placed," the פסוק about produce becoming susceptible
It will be rinsed
Wall

phrases.english: As we learned in a Mishnah:
One who turns a bowl over on the wall
so that it will be rinsed,
phrases.notes: So that the rain will rinse the bowl.

phrases.english: this falls under "when water is placed,"
if it is so that the wall won't be damaged,
it does not fall under "when water is placed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the claim that תנאים disagree.
steps.raayaObject: There is a dispute between תנאים about הכשר with something detached and later attached.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה מכשירין 4:3, about a bowl on a wall.

steps.title: The משנה seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out a problem inside the משנה. The first case suggests that if the bowl was placed to rinse the wall, it would not count under "כי יותן."
steps.simpleTranslation: This משנה itself is difficult. You said: so that it will be rinsed, it falls under "when water is placed." That implies: if it is so that the wall will be rinsed, it does not fall under "when water is placed."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts showing that the משנה seems to contradict itself. Here it draws an inference from the first case; the clash with the second case will be spelled out next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case says only the bowl being rinsed counts, which suggests that rinsing the wall would not count. The second case excludes only 'so the wall won't be damaged,' which suggests that rinsing the wall would count. The two halves point in opposite directions.

keyTerms.meaning: This source itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)
By implication; this implies that

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the change from שֶׁתּוּדַח (so that IT, the bowl, will be rinsed) to שֶׁיּוּדַח הַכּוֹתֶל (so that the WALL will be rinsed). The whole difficulty depends on which thing is being rinsed.

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
You said: so that it will be rinsed,
this falls under "when water is placed,"
which implies: if it is so that the wall will be rinsed,
this does not fall under "when water is placed."
phrases.notes: The wall is attached to the ground, so water meant for it wouldn't count.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the internal consistency of the משנה that was just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה about the bowl on the wall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The inference from the first case (rinsing the wall does not count) clashes with what the second case implies, which is spelled out next.

steps.title: The second clause implies the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The second clause of the משנה implies that if the bowl was placed so the wall gets rinsed, it does count under "כי יותן," which contradicts the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: And then the משנה teaches: if he did it so the wall would not be damaged, it is not under "כי יותן." That implies that if he did it so the wall would be rinsed, it is under "כי יותן."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its question. It shows that the second half of the משנה implies the exact opposite of what the first half implied.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause hinted that rinsing the wall does not count. The second clause hints that rinsing the wall does count. Both clauses are in the same משנה, so we need to explain how they fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: And then it teaches, pointing to a later clause in the same source
Will be damaged or harmed
Will be rinsed or washed
Implying that; an inference from the wording

phrases.english: And then it teaches:
phrases.notes: This is the second half of the same משנה we saw in step 19.

phrases.english: so that the wall will not be damaged –
it is not under "when [water] is placed,"
implying: so that the wall will be rinsed –
that is under "when [water] is placed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contradiction that step 20 began
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the משנה about the bowl on the wall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause implies that rinsing the wall does not count under "כי יותן," and the second clause implies that it does.

steps.title: Two different תנאים wrote the two clauses
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the משנה is broken: one תנא wrote the first clause and a different תנא wrote the second.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: It is broken. The one who taught this clause did not teach that clause.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the contradiction by saying the two halves of the משנה come from two תנאים who disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two clauses really do disagree about whether a wall counts as attached to the ground or as detached. This is exactly what רבא said in step 18: for הכשר זרעים, something detached and later attached is a dispute between תנאים.

keyTerms.meaning: It is broken; the משנה does not come from one author

keyTerms.term: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: The one who taught this did not teach that; two different authors

steps.whyThisMatters: This answer is the proof for רבא's claim in step 18 that the status of something detached and later attached is a dispute between תנאים.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said: It is broken,
phrases.notes: He means the משנה is split, with each clause coming from a different author.

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ.
phrases.english: the one who taught this did not teach that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in steps 20 and 21
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the source between two תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole משנה comes from one תנא, so its two clauses contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two תנאים disagree about whether a built wall counts as attached or detached, and each wrote one clause.

steps.title: One תנא: a cave wall versus a built wall
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says one תנא wrote the whole משנה. The first clause is about a cave wall, and the second is about a wall that was built.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The whole משנה is one תנא. This clause is about a cave wall, and that clause is about a built wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a different answer. He keeps the משנה as one opinion by saying each clause is talking about a different kind of wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cave wall was always part of the ground, so it is truly attached. A built wall is made of stones that were once detached and were later attached. The one תנא holds that the built wall still counts as detached, so the two clauses no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: One תנא; a single author for the whole source
A cave wall, which was always attached to the ground
A built wall, made from stones that were once detached

steps.confusionAlert: רב פפא's reading takes away רבא's proof. רבא brought this משנה to show that תנאים disagree about something detached and later attached. According to רב פפא, the whole משנה is one תנא, and it treats a built wall as detached, so this משנה shows no dispute at all.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
The whole of it is one tanna,
this is about the wall of a cave,
phrases.notes: This refers to the first clause, which hinted that rinsing the wall does not count.

phrases.english: that is about the wall of a building.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: כּוּלָּהּ חַד תַּנָּא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from רבי אלעזר's
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses are talking about the same kind of wall, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause is about a cave wall, which is always attached. The second is about a built wall, which counts as detached.

steps.title: Rereading the first clause as a cave wall
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains the first clause: on a cave wall, placing the bowl so the bowl gets rinsed counts, but placing it so the wall gets rinsed does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what it is saying: one who turns a bowl over on the wall so that the bowl will be rinsed, that is under "כי יותן." But if it is so that the wall will be rinsed, that is not under "כי יותן."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out how רב פפא reads the משנה, starting with the first clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the cave-wall case, wanting the water to rinse the bowl counts, because the bowl is a detached item. Wanting the water to rinse the cave wall does not count, because that wall was always part of the ground.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what it means; introduces a rereading of the source
One who turns a bowl upside down
When water is placed; the פסוק that makes produce able to become טמא once water touches it

phrases.english: And this is what it is saying:
one who turns a bowl over on the wall
so that it will be rinsed –
that is under "when [water] is placed,"
implying: so that the wall will be rinsed –
that is not under "when [water] is placed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out רב פפא's reading of the first clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first clause is talking about every kind of wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause is talking only about a cave wall, which is attached, so rinsing it does not count.

steps.title: A built wall: rinsing it counts
steps.stepSummary: The first rule applies only to a cave wall. For a built wall, only protecting the wall fails to count, while rinsing the wall does count under "כי יותן."
steps.simpleTranslation: When is this said? About a cave wall. But for a built wall, it is only when he did it so the wall would not be damaged that it is not under "כי יותן." If he did it so the wall would be rinsed, it is under "כי יותן."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב פפא's reading. It limits the first rule to cave walls and explains the second clause as being about built walls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A built wall is made of stones that were once detached, so this תנא treats it as detached. That is why wanting water to rinse it counts under "כי יותן," just like wanting water to rinse the bowl. Only protecting the wall from damage is not counted as wanting the water.

keyTerms.meaning: When is this said? Introduces a limit on a rule
Something detached and later attached, like the stones of a built wall

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אלעזר: two תנאים disagree about a built wall, which supports רבא. רב פפא: one תנא. A cave wall is attached, so rinsing it does not count. A built wall counts as detached, so rinsing it does count under "כי יותן."

phrases.english: In what case are these words said?
In the case of a cave wall,
but in the case of a built wall –
so that the wall will not be damaged
that is when it is not under "when [water] is placed,"
but so that the wall will be rinsed –
that is under "when [water] is placed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב פפא's reading by explaining the second clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second clause clashes with the first.
steps.terutzMaskana: The second clause is about a built wall, which counts as detached, so rinsing it counts under "כי יותן."

steps.title: רבא introduces a new question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא announces that רבא is raising a בעיא. The actual question follows in the next lines.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked a question:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is telling us that רבא is about to ask a real question that he does not know the answer to. The question itself comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בָּעֵי signals a genuine question, not an attack on someone's view. The earlier back-and-forth about the cave wall and the built wall is finished. Now the גמרא turns to something new that רבא wants to clarify.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked. This is used when a sage raises a genuine question he wants answered, not an objection.
A question of this kind, an open legal question waiting for an answer.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read בָּעֵי as a קשיא. רבא is not attacking anyone. He is honestly asking what the הלכה is.

phrases.english: Rava raises a dilemma:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב פפא resolved the contradiction in the משנה, the גמרא moves on to a new question asked by רבא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Not stated yet. This line only introduces the question, which appears in the next lines.
